title: Vulvar Lump - Bartholin Abscess with Vulval Malignancy Differentials
patient_instructions: You are Sandra Kelly, a 34-year-old woman who has noticed a painful lump near the opening of the vagina on the right side over the last 3 days. It has become swollen, tender and hot, and it now hurts to sit and to walk. You feel a bit feverish but have not measured your temperature. There is no ulcer and no bleeding from the lump. If asked: no unusual vaginal discharge, no weight loss, no other lumps. You are sexually active with one regular partner, no known STIs, last cervical screening was normal 2 years ago. You are otherwise well, not pregnant, not immunocompromised, no diabetes. You have not had this before. Your ideas: you think it might be an infected 'gland' or a cyst. Your concerns: it is very painful and you are worried it could be something serious like cancer because your aunt had 'a cancer down there'. Your expectation: you want the pain sorted and to know it is not cancer. You are uncomfortable and keen for relief. If the candidate recommends a procedure, ask 'Will I need antibiotics as well?' and 'Could this be cancer?'
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice / GP procedure room. Sandra Kelly, 34, presents with a 3-day painful swelling at the vaginal introitus. In 8 minutes: take a focused history, examine (verbalise your approach) or interpret the finding of a tender fluctuant right posterolateral vulval swelling consistent with a Bartholin abscess, explain your diagnosis and differential to the patient, and outline definitive management and safety-netting. Address her concern about cancer.
examiner_instructions: This tests management of a Bartholin abscess AND the discipline not to anchor - a suspicious/ulcerated/fixed vulval lesion needs biopsy. The finding is a tender, fluctuant right posterolateral (4 or 8 o'clock) vulval swelling. Reward: describing the lesion (site by clock position, size, tenderness, fluctuance, discharge); recognising that DEFINITIVE treatment of a Bartholin abscess is drainage with Word catheter insertion or marsupialisation (simple incision and drainage alone has high recurrence). Reward the point that antibiotics are NOT routinely required and are reserved for surrounding cellulitis, systemic sepsis, pregnancy, immunocompromise, recurrence or age over 40 (guided by swab). Reward stating that any suspicious/irregular/ulcerated/non-healing lesion, or recurrent abscess in a woman over 40, needs urgent gynae-oncology referral and biopsy - malignancy cannot be excluded on appearance alone. Reward sepsis safety-netting and HPV/Gardasil context. Prompt: 'Does she need antibiotics?'

criteria: Characterises the lump (onset, site, pain, discharge, systemic/fever symptoms) and takes a relevant sexual/STI and cervical screening history
Screens red flags for malignancy (irregular/ulcerated/non-healing lesion, bloody discharge, weight loss, age >40, recurrence)
Describes appropriate examination: lesion site by clock position, size, tenderness, fluctuance, discharge, and lesion swab if discharging
Identifies Bartholin abscess as the leading diagnosis
Gives a differential including Bartholin cyst, vulval malignancy (SCC/VIN/melanoma/Paget), cyst of canal of Nuck, lipoma, inguinal/femoral hernia and lymphadenopathy
Recognises malignancy cannot be excluded on appearance alone - biopsy any solid/fixed/ulcerated lesion
Definitive management: drainage with Word catheter or marsupialisation (not simple I&D alone) plus analgesia (paracetamol +/- NSAID)
Antibiotics NOT routine - reserved for cellulitis, sepsis, pregnancy, immunocompromise, recurrence or age >40, guided by swab
Safety-nets sepsis (fever, rigors, spreading cellulitis -> ED/IV antibiotics) and arranges biopsy/urgent gynae-oncology referral for suspicious or recurrent >40 lesions
Explains diagnosis and procedure in lay terms and gains consent
Directly and honestly addresses the cancer concern and checks understanding

red_flags: Irregular, ulcerated, fixed or non-healing vulval lesion or bloody/brown discharge - urgent gynae-oncology referral and biopsy (SCC/VIN/melanoma/Paget cannot be excluded clinically)
Recurrent Bartholin abscess in a woman over 40 - biopsy to exclude carcinoma of the gland
Systemic sepsis (fever, rigors, spreading cellulitis) requiring ED review and IV antibiotics
Rapidly enlarging or hard/fixed groin/vulval lump suggesting malignant lymphadenopathy
australian_guidelines: RANZCOG/RACGP: definitive treatment of a Bartholin abscess is drainage with Word catheter insertion or marsupialisation; simple incision and drainage alone has a high recurrence rate

eTG antibiotic guidance: antibiotics are NOT routinely required for an uncomplicated Bartholin abscess - reserve for surrounding cellulitis, systemic sepsis, pregnancy, immunocompromise, recurrence or age >40, guided by swab (cover gonorrhoea/chlamydia and MRSA where relevant)
Any suspicious vulval lesion requires diagnostic (incisional/punch) biopsy and urgent gynae-oncology referral; do not diagnose or exclude malignancy on appearance alone
National Immunisation Program: recommend Gardasil 9 HPV vaccination; VIN is a premalignant precursor requiring biopsy
learning_objectives: Diagnose and definitively manage a Bartholin abscess (Word catheter/marsupialisation) rather than simple I&D
Apply appropriate, non-routine antibiotic use for Bartholin abscess
Maintain a broad vulval-lump differential and biopsy any suspicious lesion
Recognise and safety-net systemic sepsis and vulval malignancy red flags
key_points: Definitive treatment of a Bartholin abscess is Word catheter or marsupialisation; simple I&D alone recurs frequently
Antibiotics are not routine - reserve for cellulitis, sepsis, pregnancy, immunocompromise, recurrence or age >40
Never exclude malignancy on appearance; biopsy any solid, fixed, ulcerated or non-healing vulval lesion
Recurrent Bartholin abscess in a woman over 40 warrants biopsy to exclude gland carcinoma
Offer HPV (Gardasil 9) vaccination and safety-net for sepsis

citations.claim: Bartholin cyst/abscess is managed by drainage with marsupialisation to reduce recurrence, and a focal vulval lesion should be biopsied.
Serious not-to-be-missed causes of a vulval lump include neoplasia (VIN, squamous cell carcinoma, Paget disease and melanoma), so an irregular ulcerated lesion must be worked up for malignancy.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2629

citations.claim: Red-flag features of a malignant lump - hard, irregular, ulcerated, with skin change and abnormal discharge - warrant urgent assessment.
